exercises.approach: Put colour = group and shape = group inside the global aes, add geom_point, and set the two hex values with scale_colour_manual.
exercises.why: group is a factor with levels A and B, so the scale maps the two A rows to #0072B2 and the two B rows to #D55E00. Mapping shape as well gives a second cue that survives a grayscale print.
exercises.wrong: Writing geom_point(colour = group) outside aes. The layer looks for an object called group in the calling environment, not in d, and stops with object group not found.

exercises.approach: Pass colour = "#0072B2" as an argument to geom_point, outside aes, in a second plot called constant.
exercises.why: An argument outside aes is a setting, so every one of the four rows gets the same blue and no legend is created. The mapped plot instead sends group through a scale, which is what produces two colours and a legend.
exercises.wrong: Writing aes(colour = "#0072B2"). ggplot treats the hex string as a category, draws all points in the default hue for a single level, which is not blue, and adds a legend titled with the hex code.
exercises.verify: `length(unique(ggplot2::ggplot_build(constant)$data[[1]]$colour))` returns 1, while the same expression for mapped returns 2.

exercises.approach: Build means with aggregate(cbind(x, y) ~ group, d, mean), then add geom_point(data = means, aes(x, y), inherit.aes = FALSE) with a fixed black cross.
exercises.why: Group A holds x = 1, 2 and y = 1, 3, so its mean point is (1.5, 2). Group B holds x = 3, 4 and y = 2, 6, giving (3.5, 4). The second layer therefore has exactly two rows, separate from the four raw points.
exercises.wrong: Adding geom_point(aes(y = mean(y))) to the raw data. The aesthetic is evaluated over all four rows at once, so it draws four marks at the overall mean 3 instead of two marks at 2 and 4.

exercises.approach: Read aes(colour = "group") as a constant string being mapped, and replace it with the bare column name, aes(colour = group).
exercises.why: Inside aes a quoted value is one literal repeated for every row, so all four points share one level called group and one colour. The bare name refers to the column, whose two levels give two colours.
exercises.wrong: Moving the quoted string outside aes as geom_point(colour = "group"). That turns it into a setting, and since group is not a colour name the build fails instead of showing the categories.
exercises.verify: `length(unique(ggplot2::ggplot_build(literal)$data[[1]]$colour))` returns 1, compared with 2 for the mapped plot.

exercises.approach: Store each plot in an object and call print(mapped) and print(layered) explicitly.
exercises.why: A ggplot object is only a description until it is printed. Top level autoprinting does not happen inside a function body, a for loop, or a file run with source and default arguments, so explicit print is what reaches the device.
exercises.wrong: Looping with `for (g in list(mapped, layered)) g`. The loop evaluates each object and discards it, so the device stays blank and the script still exits cleanly.
exercises.verify: Running the reference under Rscript shows two pages in the output device, one for each print call.

exercises.approach: Keep the build assertions and add a visual review of the delivered image as a separate step.
exercises.why: ggplot_build confirms four marks, two colours, two shapes and mean coordinates 2 and 4. It would pass in the same way if the axis titles still read x and y, as they do in mapped, or if the crosses hid a raw point.
exercises.wrong: Treating the colourblind friendly pair #0072B2 and #D55E00 as proof of accessibility. The palette helps, but legend size, label text and contrast against the panel background can only be judged on the rendered figure.
exercises.verify: A browser screenshot shows the legend keys, axis titles and black crosses legible at classroom size.

run_note: The starter holds four rows with x from 1 to 4, y values 1, 3, 2 and 6, and a factor group with A for the first two rows and B for the last two, and an empty results list. Run it and decide which aesthetics are mapped from columns and which are fixed settings before writing any layer. A mapping belongs inside `aes()` and names a column; a fixed colour belongs outside it, and quoting the column name inside `aes()` maps a constant string instead.
checks_note: The assertions confirm that the mapped plot builds four points with two colours and two shapes, that a constant colour set outside `aes()` produces one colour, that a mean layer with its own data adds two points at 2 and 4 beside the four raw points, and that `aes(colour = "group")` yields a single colour because it maps a literal string. They inspect built data, not the rendered image.
